sections.title: Rhythm Based ACLS
items: Start CPR, give oxygen, and attach monitor/defibrillator.
Check rhythm q2 min.
If VF / pulseless VT:
- Shock, resume CPR for 2 min, and get IV/IO access.
- If still shockable, shock again and resume CPR.
- Give epinephrine 1 mg IV/IO q3-5 min during ongoing CPR.
- If still shockable after next cycle, shock again, resume CPR, then give amiodarone 300 mg IV/IO or lidocaine.
- Continue shock -> CPR -> meds -> treat reversible causes.
If asystole / PEA:
- Resume CPR for 2 min, get IV/IO access, and give epinephrine 1 mg IV/IO q3-5 min.
- Recheck rhythm q2 min and continue CPR.
- Treat reversible causes throughout.
Airway / monitoring:
- prepare advanced airway when it will not interrupt compressions.
- Use waveform capnography to confirm tube placement and monitor CPR quality.
CPR:
- Rate 100-120/min, depth at least 2 inches, full recoil, minimal pauses, avoid overventilation.
- 30:2 if no advanced airway; if advanced airway is in place, give 1 breath q6 sec with continuous compressions.

Use POCUS; if present, get ROSC, then pericardiocentesis.
If ROSC & ACS is likely, get ECG & move toward cath lab.
If RV strain & PE is likely, consider alteplase 100 mg IV & continue CPR for 60-90 minutes afterward.
Review MAR & exposures; give antidotes (naloxone, glucagon) when indicated.

sections.title: STEMI vs NSTEMI vs Unstable Angina

pairs.value: STE in 2+ contiguous leads or STEMI equivalent. Do not wait for troponin. Activate cath lab now.
Troponin elevated without ST elevation. May have ST depression or T-wave inversion. Urgent, not immediate cath.
Ischemic symptoms with normal troponin. Still ACS: admit and risk-stratify.
Wellens, de Winter, posterior MI, or Sgarbossa-positive LBBB/paced rhythm.

images.caption: Anterior STEMI (LAD occlusion)
images.description: STE in V1V4. Reciprocal ST depression in inferior leads (II, III, aVF). Large territory: risk of cardiogenic shock & arrhythmia.

images.caption: Inferior STEMI (RCA occlusion)
images.description: ST elevation in II, III, aVF with reciprocal ST depression in I & aVL. Always get V4R to check for RV involvement & V7V9 for posterior extension.

images.caption: Wellens Syndrome (critical proximal LAD stenosis)
images.description: Deep, symmetric Twave inversions in V2V3 (Type A) or biphasic T waves in V2 (Type B). Patient is pain-free when this pattern appears. Do NOT stress test: go directly to cath. Represents critical proximal LAD stenosis with risk of anterior wall MI.

images.caption: de Winter T Waves (LAD occlusion equivalent)
images.description: Upsloping ST depression >1mm at Jpoint in V1V6 with tall, prominent, symmetric T waves. No ST elevation. This is STEMI equivalent: activate cath lab. Present in 2% of LAD occlusions.

images.caption: Sgarbossa Criteria (STEMI in LBBB)
images.description: In LBBB or paced rhythm: (1) concordant STE ≥1 mm in any lead = 5 pts, (2) concordant ST depression ≥1 mm in V1V3 = 3 pts, (3) discordant STE ≥5 mm (modified: ratio >0.25 of preceding S wave) = 2 pts. Score ≥3 is highly specific for MI.

images.caption: Posterior STEMI
images.description: ST depression in V1V3 with tall, broad R waves & upright T waves: mirror image of posterior STE. Confirm with posterior leads V7V9 showing ST elevation ≥0.5 mm. Often accompanies inferior STEMI.

pairs.value: STE in V1-V4. Large territory: risk of cardiogenic shock, CHF, arrhythmia.
STE in I, aVL, V5-V6. Often smaller infarct but can extend.
STE in II, III, aVF. Check RV involvement (V4R) & posterior (V7-V9). High vagal tone: ↓ HR common.
ST depression V1-V3, tall R waves, upright T waves in V1-V3. Confirm with V7-V9 showing STE.
Inferior STEMI + ↓ BP + clear lungs + JVD. Get V4R. NO nitrates & diuretics: preload dependent. Treat with IV fluids.
ST depression in leads opposite to STE: ↑ specificity for true STEMI. Absence does not rule it out.
[MD CALC Heart Score](https://www.mdcalc.com/calc/1752/heartscoremajorcardiacevents) Score 03: low risk, consider discharge. 4-6: moderate, admit. 7-10: high risk, early invasive.
Predicts inhospital & 6month mortality. High risk (>140): early invasive strategy within 24h. Intermediate (109140): invasive within 72h. Low (<109): ischemiaguided.
[MD CALC TIMI Score](https://www.mdcalc.com/calc/111/timiriskscoreuanstemi) Higher score = more benefit from early invasive.

sections.title: Management
items: CHECK NOW
-**Labs:** HS-troponin x2 (0h & +1h), BMP, CBC, coags, BNP, fasting lipids
-**Orders:** EKG now + serial (q15-30 min), aspirin 325 mg PO, IV access x2, telemetry, continuous SpO2, CXR
Aspirin 325mg PO Load NOW
EKG: if STEMI, then cath lab now
hstroponin: now & at +1 hour or +3 hours
Delta 15 ng/L (up OR down) – approx 20%. Delta can down as troponin will ↓ after ACS event. +ACS if >15ng/L change
IV access, telemetry, pulse ox
O2 only if SpO2 <90%: routine O2 may ↑ mortality
Nitroglycerin 0.4 mg SL q5min x3 for pain (STOP if SBP <100, RV/inferior MI, or PDE5 inhibitor use)
Heparin: UFH bolus + gtt
BB: metoprolol tartrate 12.525 mg PO (HR >60, SBP >100, no shock): avoid IV BB
Statin: atorvastatin 80 mg PO or Rosuvastatin 40mg PO
P2Y12i (HOLD if CABG possible): ticagrelor 180 mg load > clopidogrel 600 mg (c/s Cards first)

sections.title: STEMI Reperfusion Strategy
items: Primary PCI (preferred): door-balloon <90 minutes
Fibrinolytics (if PCI not available within 120 min): tenecteplase (weight based IV bolus)
Fibrinolytic CI: active bleeding, prior hemorrhagic stroke, ischemic stroke <3 months, aortic dissection, intracranial neoplasm, known bleeding diathesis
After fibrinolytics: transfer for angiography within 324 hours regardless of reperfusion success
Failed reperfusion (persistent STE + pain 60-90 min post-lytic): rescue PCI ASAP

drugs.name: Aspirin
drugs.notes: Nonenteric coated for loading. Give now to all ACS. Lifelong therapy.

drugs.name: Ticagrelor
drugs.notes: Preferred P2Y12 inhibitor in most ACS (PLATO trial). Hold 5 days before CABG. Don't use with ASA >100 mg/day.

drugs.name: Clopidogrel
drugs.notes: Alternative if ticagrelor not tolerated. Hold 5 days before CABG. CYP2C19 poor metabolizers may not respond.

drugs.name: Heparin (UFH)
drugs.notes: Target aPTT 1.5-2.5x control. Preferred if cath lab activation likely (shorter halflife, reverse with protamine).

drugs.name: Enoxaparin
drugs.notes: Alternative to UFH in NSTEMI. Reduce to 1 mg/kg daily if CrCl <30. Avoid if CABG planned within 24h.

drugs.name: Nitroglycerin
drugs.dose: 0.4 mg SL q5min x3, then IV drip 5-200 mcg/min

drugs.name: Metoprolol Tartrate
drugs.dose: 12.5-25 mg PO q6h, then 200 mg daily
drugs.notes: Start within 24h if stable. Avoid if HR <60, SBP <100, PR >0.24s, severe bronchospasm.

drugs.name: Atorvastatin
drugs.contraindications: Active hepatic disease, pregnancy, unexplained persistent ↑ transaminases
drugs.notes: Highintensity statin for all ACS. Start regardless of baseline LDL. Check LFTs, CK at baseline.

drugs.name: Tenecteplase
drugs.notes: Fibrinolytic for STEMI when PCI not available within 120 min. <60 kg: 30 mg, 60-70: 35 mg, 70-80: 40 mg, 80-90: 45 mg, >90: 50 mg.

pairs.value: SBP <90 after fluids, s/s endorgan damage. Large anterior MI. Inotropes (dobutamine), vasopressors (norepinephrine), mechanical support (IABP, Impella). Emergent cath.
VT/VF MCC of early death ACLS. Reperfusion arrhythmias (accelerated idioventricular rhythm) = benign. Complete heart block in inferior MI= temporary pacing.
Papillary muscle rupture (usually posteromedial, 27 days postMI). New loud murmur + flash pulmonary edema. Emergent surgery.
New harsh holosystolic murmur + hemodynamic collapse, 35 days post-MI. Confirm with echo + stepup in O2 sat from RA to RV. Emergent surgery.
Sudden PEA arrest 35 days post-MI. Pericardial tamponade on POCUS. Usually fatal: emergent surgery if caught.
Days to weeks postMI. Pleuritic chest pain, friction rub, diffuse ST elevation. NSAIDs + colchicine. Avoid anticoagulation if large effusion.

nl. initial troponin does NOT r/o ACS: serial troponins are essential (0/1h or 0/3h protocol)
Type 2 MI (supplydemand mismatch, anemia, sepsis, etc.) is NOT same as Type 1 MI (plaque rupture): tx differs significantly
Cocaine chest pain: Use benzodiazepines, nitroglycerin, CCBs
RV infarct triad: ↓ BP + clear lungs + JVD: give fluids, avoid nitrates & diuretics

sections.title: EKG Interpretation
items: **AFib**: No P waves, irregularly irregular RR intervals
**AFL with RVR**: Sawtooth flutter waves (best seen in II, III, aVF, V1), regular or regularly irregular rate —150 bpm (2:1 block)
**If regular**: Consider escape rhythm vs complete heart block (CHB): not true AFib
**DDx**: MAT (3+ distinct Pwave morphologies, irregular), sinus tach with frequent PACs (look for P waves before each QRS)

sections.title: Etiology / Precipitants
items: **Cardiac**: ACS/ischemia, heart failure (too much or too little fluid: Starling curve), valvular disease, hypertensive heart disease
**Pulmonary**: PE, COPD exacerbation, hypoxia, pneumonia
**Stressinduced / sympathetic surge**: Postop, sepsis, pain, hyperthyroidism, cocaine/stimulants, pheochromocytoma
**Metabolic**: Low Mg, low K, thyrotoxicosis, severe anemia
**Toxic**: Acute alcohol, alcohol withdrawal, caffeine excess, sympathomimetic drugs

sections.title: Management
items: CHECK NOW
-**Labs:** BMP (K+, Mg2+), CBC, TSH, troponin, BNP, digoxin level (if on digoxin)
-**Orders:** EKG, telemetry, IV access, continuous SpO2, TTE (if new AFib or hemodynamically compromised)
check hemodynamic stability
Unstable > immediate synchronized cardioversion; Biphasic waveform, 200 J initial energy
If stable: IV rate control
- Firstline: Beta blocker OR diltiazem (if EF >40%)
- Adjunct: IV magnesium
- Alternative: Digoxin or IV amiodarone (if HFrEF or other agents contraindicated)
- Avoid: Calcium channel blockers in moderatesevere LV dysfunction
- Avoid: AV nodal blockers in preexcitation (WPW)
Consider rhythm control (cardioversion)
- Electrical or pharmacological (ibutilide, amiodarone, flecainide/propafenone)
Anticoagulation check
- AF >48 hours: Requires 3 weeks anticoagulation OR TEE before cardioversion
- Continue anticoagulation >=4 weeks postcardioversion
Target heart rate
- Lenient: <110 bpm at rest (asymptomatic, preserved LV function)
- Strict: <=80 bpm at rest (symptomatic pts)
Check triggers and long term strategy
check precipitants (infection, electrolytes, thyroid, alcohol)
Determine CHA2DS2VASc score for long term anticoagulation

sections.title: Stable: Rate Control Protocol
items: Trial IVF 500mL-1L NS if c/f hypovolemia
Metoprolol 5mg IV q5min x3 (if HR >130 or symptomatic & sBP >90): PO metoprolol 25mg PO q6h (max 400mg/day)
Diltiazem 0.25 mg/kg IV bolus (max 25mg): can rebolus after 15 min: drip 2.5-5 mg/hr: PO ER dose = 10 x [3(infusion rate mg/hr) + 3], max 360mg/day
AVOID diltiazem/verapamil in decompCHF (EF <40%): use amiodarone or digoxin
Digoxin: load 250 mcg q2-6h, then 125-375 mcg daily. Onset 1h, peak 1-6h. Good for CHF + AFib. Avoid in CKD/ Abn [K]
Abx if c/f sepsis
Amiodarone if rate control fails or rhythm control is desired (see rhythm section)

sections.title: Rhythm Control: Amiodarone
items: On AC for 3 weeks OR 100% confirmed new AFib <48h
IV load: 150mg bolus over 10 min: can repeat
IV drip: 1 mg/min x 6 hours: then 0.5 mg/min x 18 hours (full IV load = 10g)
Transition to PO: 400mg PO TID until 10g total load, then 200mg PO BID maintenance
Watch for: ↓BP with rapid IV bolus, ↓HR, phlebitis, long term thyroid/pulm/hepatic tox
Can cause stroke if pt converts to sinus rhythm & is not anticoagulated: make sure AC on board

sections.title: Unstable: Synchronized Cardioversion
items: Indications: hemodynamic instability (↓ BP, shock, AMS, active ischemia, pulmonary edema)
Give 2 mg midazolam + 25 mcg fentanyl (will need more if tolerant)
Apply pads: anteriorposterior preferred
Select SYNC mode on defibrillator: confirm Synch marker on R waves
AFib: 200J biphasic; AFL: 50-100J biphasic
If unsuccessful: reconfirm SYNC mode is on
WARNING: if pt not anticoagulated & sx onset >48h or unknown. cardiovert risk of stroke

sections.title: AC Strategy
items: **CHA2DS2VASc**: 1 point each for CHF, HTN, age 6574, DM, female sex, vascular disease; 2 points for age >75 & prior stroke/TIA
**Score 0 (male)**: No AC needed
**Score 1 (male)**: Consider AC
**Score >2**: Anticoagulation suggested (DOAC > warfarin for nonsevere MS AFib)
**Precardioversion**: If <48h onset, cardiovert without TEE & continue AC 4 weeks after; if >48h or unknown, get TEE or therapeutic AC for 3 weeks first
**Postcardioversion**: Continue AC for 4 weeks regardless of CHA2DS2VASc

sections.title: Initial Workup
items: EKG ASAP
Labs: CBC, BMP, Mg/Phos, TSH, LFTs, coagulation studies, troponin, NTproBNP
Consider UDS (cocaine, stimulants)
CXR: pulmonary edema, vascular congestion
POCUS: LV function, LA/RA size, valve disease, pulmonary HTN, LV thrombus

drugs.name: Metoprolol
drugs.dose: 5mg IV q5min x3, then 12.5-25mg PO q6h
drugs.notes: Firstline rate control if no decompensated CHF. Max 400mg/day PO. Avoid if HR <60, SBP <90, active bronchospasm, 2nd/3rd degree AV block.

drugs.name: Diltiazem
drugs.dose: 0.25 mg/kg IV bolus (max 25mg), rebolus x1 after 15 min, then 2.5-5 mg/hr drip
drugs.notes: PO ER dose = 10 x [3(infusion rate) + 3], max 360mg/day.

drugs.name: Digoxin
drugs.dose: 250 mcg IV q2-6h (load), then 125-375 mcg daily
drugs.notes: Good for CHF + AFib (no negative inotropy). Onset 1h, peak 1-6h. Narrow therapeutic index: monitor levels & renal function.

drugs.name: Amiodarone
drugs.dose: 150mg IV over 10 min (x1-3), then 1 mg/min x6h, then 0.5 mg/min
drugs.notes: Rate & rhythm control. Use when BB/CCBs contraindicated (CHF). PO transition: 400mg BID: 200mg BID. Full load = 10g.

drugs.name: Synchronized cardioversion
drugs.contraindications: Digitalis toxicity (relative — may trigger VF), need sedation if conscious
drugs.notes: Always confirm SYNC mode ON. Sedate before if time allows. Firstline for hemodynamic instability/AMS .

sections.title: Pearls & Pitfalls
items: AFib with RVR alone rarely causes ↓ BP unless HR >150: AFib dec. preload (loss of atrial kick)
AFib ↓ preload through loss of atrial kick (up to 25% of cardiac output): esp important in diastolic dysfunction, HOCM, MS
NEVER give digoxin, diltiazem, or verapamil in WPW with AFib: can accelerate conduction down accessory pathway & cause VF
AVOID diltiazem & verapamil in decompensated CHF or EF <40%
Flutter is 2:1: if ventricular rate is exactly 150, always suspect flutter with 2:1 block
New AFib: always look for & treat precipitant: rate may resolve once sepsis, PE, hyperthyroidism treated

sections.title: Background
items: Sick sinus syndrome: dysfunction of SA node function and may also be described as sinus node dysfunction or sinoatrial node disease.
Presentations vary: persistent sinus bradycardia, sinus pauses or arrest, chronotropic incompetence, or periods of atrial tachyarrhythmia alternating with slow sinus recovery.
The tachy-brady form is common and often appears as atrial fibrillation or flutter followed by prolonged pauses when the fast rhythm terminates.
Symptoms come from low cardiac output(loose atrial kick), transient cerebral hypoperfusion, or rapid atrial arrhythmias rather than from one single ECG pattern.

pairs.value: Age-related fibrosis of the sinus node and atrial tissue, ischemic injury, infiltrative disease, remodeling after atrial arrhythmia, or less commonly ion channel disease.
Beta blockers, non-DHP calcium channel blockers, digoxin, amiodarone, other antiarrhythmics, clonidine, and similar nodal suppressing agents.
Hyperkalemia, other electrolyte disturbance, hypothyroidism, hypothermia, sleep apnea, increased vagal tone, and autonomic dysfunction.
Atrial fibrillation or flutter commonly coexists, especially in the tachy-brady phenotype.

sections.title: Typical Clinical Features
items: Syncope or near-syncope
Palpitations or an intermittent sensation of racing followed by pauses
Fatigue, exertional intolerance, or generalized weakness
Dyspnea or chest discomfort
Sleep disruption, confusion, or episodic dizziness

pairs.value: Sinus bradycardia, sinus pauses, sinoatrial exit block, sinus arrest, or failure to mount an appropriate rate with exertion.
AFib, atrial flutter, or atrial tachycardia that is followed by a prolonged pause or marked bradycardia after conversion.
A single ECG may be normal. Diagnosis often requires telemetry, Holter monitoring, event monitoring, or loop recording tied to symptoms.
Sinus tachycardia, focal atrial tachycardia, AVNRT, AVRT, atrial flutter with fixed block, or other PSVT.
AFib, atrial flutter with variable conduction, multifocal atrial tachycardia, or sinus rhythm with frequent ectopy.
Inferior MI, med toxicity, hyperkalemia, hypothyroidism, hypothermia, vasovagal episodes, increased ICP, Lyme disease, or BRASH syndrome.

sections.title: Evaluation
items: ECG now Check old ekgs for chronic sinus bradycardia, pauses, or atrial arrhythmias.
BMP, magnesium, calcium, TSH, troponin, and med review including digoxin or AV nodal blockers.
Consider ambulatory Holter, event monitor, or implantable loop recorder when episodes are intermittent.
Check for reversible causes before labeling the problem as intrinsic sinus node disease.

sections.title: Management
items: CHECK NOW
-**Labs:** BMP (K+, Mg2+), TSH, digoxin level (if applicable)
-**Orders:** EKG, telemetry, IV access, transcutaneous pacing pads on, continuous SpO2, cardiology consult
check rhythm and stability: bradycardia vs tachycardia, vitals, mentation, shock, ischemic pain, and acute heart failure.
Treat reversible causes: review nodal blocking meds, correct hypoxemia, ischemia, electrolyte problems, hypothyroidism, and metabolic derangements.
If symptomatic bradycardia or hemodynamic compromise is present:
- Atropine 0.5-1 mg IV q3-5 min up to 2 mg total; avoid in heart transplant pts without autonomic reinnervation.
- If atropine fails or is contraindicated: epinephrine 2-10 mcg/min IV, dopamine 5-20 mcg/kg/min IV, or cautious isoproterenol.
- Transcutaneous pacing is reasonable; place pads early and confirm electrical plus mechanical capture.
Use temporary transvenous pacing only for persistent unstable bradycardia refractory to medical therapy while awaiting resolution or permanent pacing.
If unstable tachyarrhythmia is present: synchronized cardioversion.
If stable narrow-complex tachycardia is present:
- Start with vagal maneuvers.
- Then consider adenosine for SVT, or diltiazem/verapamil or IV beta-blocker for rate control depending on rhythm and EF.
- In AFib/flutter, use nondihydropyridine CCBs or beta-blockers first-line; consider amiodarone if HF limits those agents.
Plan for permanent pacemaker if symptomatic bradycardia persists or recurs.
Avoid antiarrhythmics for tachycardia control until pacing is secured if bradycardia risk is high.

sections.title: Pearls & Pitfalls
items: Do not diagnose sick sinus syndrome from one isolated heart rate alone; the key issue is symptom-producing sinus node dysfunction.
Post-conversion pauses after AFib or flutter are a major clue to tachy-brady syndrome.
!!Before escalating nodal blockers for a fast atrial rhythm, ask whether pt may already have sinus node disease underneath.
Always review reversible causes before committing a pt to a permanent device!!.

sections.title: Management
items: CHECK NOW
-**Labs:** BMP (K+, Mg2+), TSH
-**Orders:** 12-lead EKG immediately, telemetry, IV access, continuous SpO2
Check hemodynamic stability
Unstable (hypotension, AMS, shock, chest pain, acute HF): immediate synchronized cardioversion
Stable: try vagal maneuvers first
- Modified Valsalva: strain, then passive leg raise supine
- Carotid sinus massage only after confirming no bruit
If vagal maneuvers fail: give IV adenosine
Keep pt on a cardiac monitor with pads available
Avoid adenosine in preexcited AF, severe asthma, or post-heart transplant pts
If adenosine fails or is contraindicated: use IV diltiazem, verapamil, or beta blocker when appropriate
Avoid AV nodal blockers if preexcitation or VT is suspected
If refractory: consider cardioversion or antiarrhythmic therapy
**ECG:** during tachycardia & after conversion: compare to prior
**BMP + Mg:** Lyte abnormalities (K, Mg, Ca) can precipitate or sustain SVT
**CBC:** Check for anemia as a trigger
**Troponin:** If chest pain, ischemic concern, or prolonged tachycardia
**TSH:** If unexplained/recurrent SVT or hyperthyroid features
**As indicated:** CXR, infectious workup, VBG/ABG, lactate, tox screen: only if suggested by presentation
**Monitoring:** telemetry, pulse ox, frequent BP. Defib pads early if sx or marginal

sections.title: Practical Modified Valsalva
items: For cooperative stable pt only
Sit pt semirecumbent
Have pt blow forcefully into syringe for ~15 seconds
Immediately lay pt flat & raise legs to ~45° for ~15 seconds
Return upright & recheck rhythm
Modified Valsalva has better conversion rates than standard Valsalva (AAFP evidence review)

sections.title: Cardioversion: Step by Step
items: Confirm pt has pulse & tachycardia is causing instability
Call for more support, place pt on monitor/defib with pads attached
Make sure suction, O2, IV access, & airway equipment at bedside
Turn on SYNC mode: verify sync markers tracking each QRS. Resync after each shock
Set 100J synchronized for narrowcomplex tachycardia
Sedate if feasible (diazepam ± fentanyl)
Clear pt & deliver synchronized shock
Recheck rhythm, pulse, BP, mentation, sx NOW. Get postconversion ECG
If in tachycardia: reenable SYNC, escalate energy, consider antiarrhythmic, consult cardiology/ICU
If sync delayed & pt crashing: proceed to unsynchronized shocks

drugs.name: Adenosine
drugs.dose: attach pads: 6mg rapid IVP, then 12mg rapid IVP if no conversion, then may repeat 12mg x1
drugs.notes: Attach to monitor/ECG before dosing. 1/2life ~10s.

drugs.name: Metoprolol tartrate
drugs.dose: 5mg IV over 1-2 min; may repeat q5min up to 15mg total
drugs.contraindications: ↓ BP, decomp HFrEF, severe ↓ HR, preexcitation, 2nd/3rd degree AVB
drugs.notes: Only if pt is truly stable. Avoid if rhythm dx uncertain

drugs.name: Diltiazem
drugs.dose: 0.25 mg/kg (~10mg) IV over 2 min; if needed 0.35 mg/kg after 15 min
drugs.contraindications: ↓ BP, decomp HFrEF, preexcitation, WPW, widecomplex tachy
drugs.notes: NonDHP CCB. Don't use with IV beta-blocker concurrently.

drugs.name: Verapamil
drugs.dose: 2.5-5mg IV slow push; may repeat carefully if needed
drugs.contraindications: ↓ BP, decomp HFrEF, preexcitation, WPW, widecomplex tachy of uncertain origin
drugs.notes: NonDHP CCB. Use cautiously: more negative inotropy than diltiazem

pairs.value: P waves & QRS complexes march independently: pathognomonic for VT

All precordial leads (V1-V6) showing same QRS direction (all positive or all negative): favors VT
"Northwest axis" (negative in I & aVF): VT
>160 ms = more likely VT; >200 ms = ↑K or Na channel blocker toxicity

Treating VT as SVT can be fatal; treating SVT as VT is rarely harmful

items: CHECK NOW

Monomorphic VT: synchronized cardioversion
Polymorphic VT: unsynchronized highenergy defibrillation
If stable: get ECG and check reversible causes
Check for ischemia, electrolyte abnormalities, and drug induced proarrhythmia
Get echocardiography to check for structural heart disease
If stable: choose pharmacologic therapy based on structural heart disease
- With structural heart disease: IV procainamide preferred; amiodarone or sotalol are alternatives
- Without structural heart disease: consider verapamil or beta blockers for idiopathic VT
Avoid verapamil/diltiazem in widecomplex tachycardia of unknown origin or myocardial dysfunction
Avoid lidocaine except possibly for acute MIrelated VT
For polymorphic VT or torsades: give IV magnesium
Correct electrolytes, especially potassium
Use overdrive pacing or isoproterenol if QT prolongation is present
Secondary prevention: consider ICD implantation
ICD indicated after VF or hemodynamically unstable VT not due to reversible causes
ICD indicated for structural heart disease with spontaneous sustained VT
Stable monomorphic VT often still warrants ICD; ablation may substitute in select cases
Longterm VT suppression in ICD pts: beta blockers first line
Amiodarone plus beta blocker is common for recurrent VT or ICD shocks
Sotalol is an alternative if no severe LV dysfunction, renal impairment, or VT storm
Mexiletine is often added for breakthrough VT
Assume wide complex tachycardia is VT until proven otherwise: 80% of WCT is VT (>90% with known cardiac disease)
Treating VT as SVT can be fatal; treating SVT as VT is rarely harmful: when in doubt, treat as VT

Procainamide > amiodarone for stable VT (PROCAMIO trial) unless acute MI or ↓ EF (n amiodarone preferred)
Very wide QRS (>200 ms) with rate <120 bpm: think ↑K before VT: give calcium first
Cannon A waves in JVP = AV dissociation = VT: quick bedside exam finding
Bidirectional VT (alternating QRS axis) is classic for digoxin toxicity: check level, give DigiFab
Electrical storm (≥3 VT episodes in 24 hrs): escalate to overdrive pacing, deep sedation, EP consult, consider ablation
Admit ALL VT pts: even if successfully cardioverted; high recurrence risk + for structural workup + ICD evaluation

drugs.name: Procainamide
drugs.dose: 20-50 mg/min IV until suppressed; max 17 mg/kg or 1 g total; maintenance 1-4 mg/min
drugs.notes: Firstline for stable monomorphic VT (PROCAMIO trial: 67% termination vs 38% for amiodarone). Monitor QRS width & BP during infusion

drugs.name: Amiodarone
drugs.dose: 150 mg IV over 10 min, then 1 mg/min × 6 hrs (360 mg), then 0.5 mg/min × 18 hrs (540 mg)
drugs.contraindications: Severe sinus node disease, 2nd/3rd degree block without pacer, cardiogenic shock
drugs.notes: Preferred if acute MI or ↓ EF. Slower onset than procainamide. Total 24hr dose ~1050 mg

drugs.name: Lidocaine
drugs.dose: 1-1.5 mg/kg IV bolus; may repeat 0.5-0.75 mg/kg q5-10 min (max 3 mg/kg); infusion 1-4 mg/min
drugs.notes: Alternative for ischemiarelated VT; fewer hemodynamic effects than procainamide. ↓ dose in liver disease & elderly

drugs.name: Magnesium sulfate
drugs.dose: 2 g IV over 5-10 min; repeat 1x PRN
drugs.notes: First for torsades de pointes; replete if Mg <2.0 in any VT

drugs.name: Adenosine (diagnostic)
drugs.dose: 6 mg rapid IV push, then 12 mg if no response
drugs.contraindications: DONT use for irregular WCT (AFib with WPW: VF risk)
drugs.notes: Diagnostic trial for regular monomorphic WCT: will NOT terminate VT but may unmask underlying SVT. Safe to give in stable pt

drugs.name: Sodium bicarbonate
drugs.notes: For Na channel blocker toxicity (TCA, cocaine) w/ wide QRS; also for ↑K with VT

>30 sec duration or causes hemodynamic compromise before 30 sec

sections.title: Initial Management by Scenario
items: Pulmonary edema + ↑ WOB: BiPAP + IV Lasix 40-80mg IV
HTN or normotensive + wet: afterload reduction (hydralazine, nitroprusside, nitroglycerin) + diuresis
↓ BP: passive leg raise or cautious 250-500mL fluid bolus: check response
H↓ BP + no CHF: 1L NS pressurebagged, recheck
↓ BP persists: start Levo, then +inotrope (dobutamine>milrinone)
Wet + cold + SBP >90: diurese + inotrope
Severe effusion contributing to low output: consider thoracentesis
Refractory to medical therapy: mechanical circulatory support (IABP, Impella, ECMO): consult cardiology/CT surgery

drugs.name: Furosemide (Lasix)
drugs.dose: 40-80mg IV (or 2.5x home PO dose if on chronic Lasix)
drugs.notes: Firstline for pulmonary edema & volume overload. Can convert to drip 5-40mg/hr for refractory overload.

drugs.name: Norepinephrine (Levophed)
drugs.notes: Firstline vasopressor in cardiogenic shock. Start BEFORE inotrope: giving inotrope first may drop BP further.

drugs.name: Dobutamine
drugs.notes: Inotrope + mild vasodilator. Use for Cold/Wet profile. Avoid if on long term BB: milrinone preferred.

drugs.name: Milrinone
drugs.notes: Inodilator (↓ afterload). Preferred if on BB. Renally cleared: use caution in AKI. Will drop BP.

drugs.name: Nitroglycerin
drugs.notes: Preload & mild afterload reduction. Useful for HTN + pulmonary edema.

drugs.name: Nitroprusside
drugs.contraindications: Hepatic failure (cyanide accumulation), renal failure, compensatory HTN (e.g., coarctation)
drugs.notes: Potent afterload reducer. Goal SVR 8001200, MAP >60. Use for severe HTN or high afterload state. Cyanide toxicity risk with prolonged use.

drugs.name: Hydralazine
drugs.contraindications: Coronary artery disease (reflex tachycardia), dissecting aneurysm, lupus (long-term risk)
drugs.notes: Oral afterload reduction. Paired with nitrates for ACE/ARBintolerant pts (BiDil regimen).

sections.title: Pearls & Pitfalls
items: AVOID intubation whenever possible in cardiogenic shock: removal of respiratory drive causes cardiovascular collapse
NEVER give inotrope before vasopressor in hypotensive cardiogenic shock: inodilators drop BP further
For pts on long term BB: milrinone is preferred inotrope (beta receptor already blocked)
Positive pressure ventilation (BiPAP/intubation) can ↑ RV afterload: use with caution in RV failure
Severe AS + cardiogenic shock: AVOID high dose afterload reducers (ACE inhibitors, high dose nitrates): pt depends on elevated afterload for coronary perfusion
Rapidly decreasing afterload in AS can precipitate cardiovascular collapse
New MR or TR murmur in ACS context = papillary muscle rupture: emergent cardiac surgery consultation
Free wall rupture postMI: emergent surgical repair
Overshooting diuresis can reduce preload excessively: worsening low output: monitor closely

sections.title: Approach: Treat the Physiology, Not the Number

pairs.value: Emergency = severe BP + acute organ injury; the number alone is not the emergency. Comfortable pt at 228/118 w/o organ injury ≠ drip; previously normotensive pt at 170/110 with seizures/PRES can be. Avoid aggressive tx of asymptomatic inpatient HTN (possible harm).
What organ am I saving? Is HTN causing the problem or the reverse? What is baseline BP? Is the BP real?

↓MAP ~20-25% in first hr → ~160/100 over 2-6 hr → normalize over 24-48 hr. Think %MAP, not SBP (MAP ≈ DBP + ⅓ pulse pressure). Chronic HTN shifts autoregulation right — 170/90 may be relative hypotension.
HOCM/LVOTO, severe AS, severe PAH/RV failure, acute ischemic stroke, hypovolemia. Check for these before reflexively lowering BP.

Don't treat 220/120 — treat 220/120 + the physiology. Dissection→esmolol then vasodilator; SCAPE→NIV+high-dose NTG; PRES→nicardipine/clevidipine; ICH→smooth SBP 130-150; AIS→usually tolerate; severe AS→cautious afterload reduction; HOCM→beta-block; PAH/RV→protect perfusion; stimulant→sedate first.
Impulse control, not just BP. 1) Esmolol first (HR <60), 2) add nicardipine/clevidipine for SBP <120 within 20 min. NO pure vasodilator before beta-blockade (reflex tachycardia ↑ shear stress).

Nicardipine or clevidipine (labetalol if drip not needed). ↓MAP 20-25% in 60 min; don't slam 240→120. MRI for PRES. Dx of exclusion (r/o hemorrhage, stroke, infection, tox/metabolic). AMS improves in hours.
SBP 130-150 acutely; avoid <130 (INTERACT2, ATACHII). Nicardipine or clevidipine. Prioritize smoothness — BP variability (205→125→190) worsens outcomes. Reverse AC; neurosurgery C/S.

Usually tolerate HTN. No reperfusion: treat only if >220/120 (lower ~15%). Pre-tPA <185/110; post-tPA <180/105. Do NOT drive SBP <140 post-thrombolysis or post-thrombectomy — no benefit, may harm (2026 AHA/ASA).

Afterload redistribution, not just volume. Sit up + early NIV (CPAP 10-15, up to ~20 if refractory). High-dose NTG: start 100-300 mcg/min, titrate up (400-800 briefly if refractory); 10-20 mcg/min is inadequate. Add clevidipine/nicardipine if still severe. Diurese/HD only if true volume overload. Maximize NIV + afterload reduction before intubating.

Not an absolute vasodilator contraindication — LV load = valve + SVR. If AS + HTN + edema: ICU, POCUS, NIV, small carefully-titrated afterload reduction; avoid abrupt preload/afterload collapse & giant NTG bolus. Hypotension is more dangerous than residual HTN (coronary perfusion of hypertrophied LV).

Vasodilators worsen obstruction — avoid NTG, nitroprusside, dihydropyridine CCB (nicardipine/clevidipine), hydralazine, ACEi/ARB, aggressive diuresis. Use non-vasodilating beta-blocker: esmolol (or metoprolol 2.5-5 mg IV). Labetalol less ideal (alpha → ↓SVR). Hypotension after nitrates/diuresis may be worsening LVOTO → stop vasodilators, cautious fluids, phenylephrine, bedside echo (2024 HCM guideline).

Systemic BP perfuses the RV — dropping it too far → RV ischemia/shock spiral. Confirm HTN is actually causing organ injury before lowering. Keep MAP >60 (norepi/vasopressin if RV failing). Avoid NTG (preload), esp. with riociguat/recent PDE5i. Don't beta-block tachycardia (supports CO). Titrate nicardipine/clevidipine very cautiously; treat RV afterload (O2, correct acidosis, avoid hypercapnia); involve PH team.

Cocaine/meth/sympathomimetics, MAOI, withdrawal. Treat adrenergic drive FIRST: benzodiazepine (lorazepam 1-2 mg or midazolam 2-5 mg IV, titrate). Then nicardipine/clevidipine, or NTG if ACS/SCAPE. Don't just chase the number.
Labetalol 20mg IV (can repeat), or hydralazine 5-10mg IV, or nicardipine gtt. Magnesium sulfate 4g IV load: 1g/hr gtt for seizure prophylaxis/tx. Definitive tx = delivery.

Phentolamine 1-5 mg IV, repeat/titrate (or nicardipine/clevidipine). NEVER beta-block before adequate alpha-blockade. Crisis/stress/pain raises metanephrines — a positive result during crisis ≠ pheo; defer renin/aldo & metanephrine workup until stabilized.

drugs.name: Nicardipine
drugs.notes: Max 15 mg/hr. CCB: titratable. Good for most hypertensive emergencies including neurologic. Accumulates — de-escalate early once at target rather than leaving pinned at max. Watch reflex tachycardia, edema, phlebitis.

drugs.name: Clevidipine
drugs.dose: Start 1-2 mg/hr, double q90sec initially; slow titration q5-10min as target approaches
drugs.notes: Max 21 mg/hr. Ultrashortacting CCB, rapid on/off — best for profoundly labile BP. Most titratable agent available. Lipid emulsion: contraindicated in egg/soy allergy, pancreatitis; triglyceride burden with prolonged/high dose.

drugs.name: Labetalol
drugs.notes: Max 300mg/24h. Alpha + beta blocker. Good for a modest controlled ↓ (not a titratable drip). Long-acting — boluses stack; not for minute-to-minute control. Good for aortic dissection (with esmolol).

drugs.name: Esmolol
drugs.dose: Load 500 mcg/kg over 1 min, then 25 mcg/kg/min; titrate to max 200 mcg/kg/min
drugs.notes: Ultrashortacting beta1 blocker. Drug of choice when HR/contractility drive the problem (dissection, HOCM/LVOTO, adrenergic tachycardia). Halflife ~9 min: easy to titrate.

drugs.name: Fenoldopam
drugs.dose: Start 0.1-0.3 mcg/kg/min, titrate by 0.1 mcg/kg/min q15min
drugs.notes: Max 1.6 mcg/kg/min. Dopamine1 agonist: enhances renal perfusion & natriuresis. Preferred if AKI present. May cause reflex tachycardia.

drugs.name: Nitroprusside
drugs.notes: Potent arterial + venous dilator. No longer routine first-line — modern titratable agents preferred (2024 BMJ). Overshoot hypotension, ↑ICP, V/Q mismatch. Cyanide toxicity with prolonged use (>4872h) or renal failure. Lightsensitive: wrap tubing.

drugs.name: Nitroglycerin
drugs.dose: Start 20-40 mcg/min; SCAPE start 100-300 mcg/min, titrate rapidly (400-800 briefly if refractory)
drugs.contraindications: PDE5i (sildenafil/vardenafil <24h, tadalafil <48h), riociguat, preload dependence, hypotension
drugs.notes: Not a general HTN infusion. Best for SCAPE & ACS. Low dose venodilates; arterial afterload reduction needs high dose.

drugs.name: Hydralazine
drugs.contraindications: Coronary artery disease (reflex tachycardia), dissecting aneurysm, lupus (long-term risk)
drugs.notes: Onset 10-20 min, duration unpredictable. Use for eclampsia/preeclampsia if labetalol/nicardipine unavailable. Avoid as first line: less titratable.

sections.title: Refractory HTN — Check Before Escalating
items: Is the BP real? Wrong/undersized cuff, cuff over clothing, tremor, a-line whip or unzeroed/unleveled line
Txt Trigger: Pain, **urinary retention**, agitation, hypoxemia/hypercapnia, n/v, alcohol/opioid/benzo/clonidine/beta-blocker withdrawal, intracranial HTN
Missed secondary driver? Dissection, SCAPE, renal failure/GN, renal artery disease, stimulants, pheo, thyroid storm, autonomic dysreflexia
Did the drug get delivered? Infiltrated IV, paused pump, wrong concentration, incompatible infusion, BP cuff not cycling
Poor drug match? NTG 20 mcg/min for SCAPE, metoprolol alone for vasoconstrictive crisis, stacked hydralazine, amlodipine when you need effect this hour, nicardipine w/o impulse control in dissection

Sequence: confirm BP → reconfirm dx & target organ → treat pain/adrenergic state → maximize ONE titratable infusion before adding agents → add complementary agent → arterial line if labile/deteriorating → recheck volume (malignant HTN → pressure natriuresis/relative hypovolemia) → bedside echo (LVOTO, AS, RV failure) → ICU

sections.title: Common Mistakes to Avoid

Treating pain-related BP before treating the pain
Restarting all home antihypertensives at once; dropping chronic severe HTN to 'normal'
Vasodilator before beta-blockade in dissection
Aggressive nitrates or diuresis in severe LVOTO; beta-blocking decompensated PAH just because HR 120

items: **Classic presentation**: Circuit failure, oxygenator clot, cannula displacement, or catastrophic bleeding in a patient on VA or VV ECMO — these are immediately life-threatening; identify whether the emergency is circuit-, cannula-, or patient-related
Cannula sites: bleeding, hematoma, signs of infection, secure dressings

Flat = hypovolemic/distributive; elevated = cardiogenic, tamponade, tension PTX, RV failure

sections.title: Management

pairs.value: Recognize shock early, secure airway and oxygenation as needed, establish IV access, start monitoring, and assess perfusion repeatedly.
Use fluids when hypovolemia or distributive shock is likely, but avoid uncritical boluses in cardiogenic or obstructive shock.
Start vasopressors early when MAP remains low after initial resuscitation; add inotropes when pump failure predominates.
Shock resolves only when the underlying process is treated: bleeding control, sepsis therapy, reperfusion, decompression, thrombolysis, or endocrine rescue as appropriate.

pairs.value: Abx + source control, 30 mL/kg LR bolus (unless CHF/renal/cirrhosis), Levo → vasopressin → epinephrine. Hydrocortisone 50 mg IV q6h + fludrocortisone 50 mg daily if on 2 pressors or AI suspected.
Epinephrine 0.3mg IM (thigh) STAT. IV fluids, diphenhydramine 50mg IV, methylprednisolone 125mg IV, H2 blocker. Epinephrine gtt if refractory.
MTP 1:1:1 (pRBC:FFP:platelets), calcium gluconate after every 4 units pRBC. Source control (endoscopy, IR, surgery).
Levo first, then inotrope (dobutamine or milrinone). BiPAP for pulmonary edema. Avoid intubation if possible. Treat cause (PCI for ACS).

Hydrocortisone 100mg IV STAT, aggressive IV fluids, correct hypoglycemia. Do not delay for labs.

drugs.name: Dobutamine

drugs.name: Hydrocortisone
drugs.contraindications: Active untreated systemic fungal infection (relative; do not delay in crisis)

drugs.name: Sodium bicarbonate

sections.title: Pearls & Pitfalls
items: Confirm BP cuff placement
Flat IVC on POCUS does not always mean hypovolemia in ventilated pt
In undifferentiated shock: treat empirically→workup. Low threshold for pressors
NEVER give inotrope BEFORE vasopressor for hypotensive cardiogenic shock(drop BP further)
Positive pressure ventilation reduces preload — use w/ caution in tamponade, RV failure
Lactic acidosis in TCA OD is from seizures and hypoperfusion — bicarb treats the cardiotoxicity, not the lactate
Adrenal crisis mimics septic shock perfectly: Consider in pts on chronic steroids or w/ known adrenal disease

sections.title: GI Hemorrhage — Special Considerations
items: Emergent upper endoscopy is first-line for most upper GI bleeds
Exception: aortic surgery within past 5 years → CT angiogram first to r/o aortoenteric fistula before scope
Exception: exsanguinating duodenal ulcer w/ active extravasation on CTA → consider IR directly (posterior duodenal ulcers difficult to control endoscopically)
MTP blood bank order: 10 units pRBC, 6 units FFP, 1 unit platelets (uncrossed)
Massive transfusion ratio: pRBC:FFP:platelets = 1:1:1 (surgical data supports 4:1:1)
Calcium gluconate after every 4 units pRBC — citrate in pRBCs chelates ionized calcium
TXA 1g IV if within 3 hours of hemorrhage onset

sections.title: Chart Check / Hx.
items: Known PAD, prior LE procedures, bypass grafts, stents — prior imaging and operative reports are critical
Atrial fibrillation (most common cardiac source of emboli), prior echo findings, LV thrombus, valvular disease, recent MI
Prior DVT/PE, hypercoagulable conditions (APS, HIT, malignancy, Factor V Leiden)
Anticoagulation use — current or recently stopped
Symptom onset timing: sudden (embolic) vs gradual over days/weeks (thrombotic in PAD)
Prior claudication or rest pain — suggests underlying PAD (thrombotic more likely)

pairs.value: Severe, sudden onset; worsens with passive movement of the extremity (ischemic muscle). Absent or blunted pain in non-viable limb (sensory nerve death) — paradoxically 'better' pain can mean worse ischemia.
Initially pale → then cyanotic and mottled (livedo) as deoxygenated blood pools. Mottling that blanches with pressure is still viable; fixed mottling that does not blanch suggests non-viability.
Absent pulses distal to occlusion. Use hand-held Doppler — arterial and venous signals. Loss of arterial Doppler signal = threatened limb. Perform bilateral comparison.
Numbness, tingling, or decreased light touch sensation. Indicates sensory nerve ischemia — urgency marker. Progresses from paresthesias → dense sensory loss → paralysis.
Motor loss — initially mild weakness, then complete paralysis. Paralysis is a late finding indicating severe ischemia; if present, revascularization is urgent or limb may already be non-viable.
Cool extremity at and distal to occlusion. Assess with back of hand; compare bilateral. A line of temperature demarcation often approximates the level of occlusion.

Check bilateral pulses (femoral, popliteal, DP, PT), cap refill, skin color, temperature, and motor/sensory exam. Doppler all four extremities. Note: regular rhythm with severe PAD may cause thrombotic ALI; irregular rhythm → embolic source.

Not immediately threatened. No sensory loss, no muscle weakness. Arterial AND venous Doppler signals present. Management: anticoagulate, urgent CTA with runoff, elective or semi-urgent revascularization planning.

Salvageable with prompt treatment. Minimal sensory loss (toes only), no muscle weakness. Venous Doppler present; arterial Doppler often absent. Management: anticoagulate, urgent CTA if safely feasible, urgent revascularization (CDT preferred if <14 days).

Salvageable with immediate intervention. Rest pain + sensory loss beyond toes + mild-moderate muscle weakness. Venous Doppler present; arterial Doppler absent. Management: to OR immediately — embolectomy or CDT. No time for CTA in most cases.

Major tissue loss or permanent nerve damage is inevitable. Dense sensory loss, paralysis, fixed skin mottling (non-blanching), absent Doppler signals (venous and arterial). Management: primary amputation; revascularization will not save limb and risks fatal reperfusion injury. Discuss goals of care.

Cardiac source most common: AFib (most frequent), LV thrombus post-MI, valvular disease, endocarditis, intracardiac tumor. Also: proximal aneurysm (popliteal most common peripheral aneurysm to embolize), paradoxical embolism (PFO + DVT). Emboli lodge at bifurcations. Onset: sudden, severe, no prior claudication, normal contralateral pulses.

Acute thrombosis on underlying PAD plaque or in-stent/graft thrombosis. History of claudication, known PAD, prior revascularization. Onset: more gradual, milder than embolic (collaterals have formed). Contralateral pulses may also be diminished. Heparin + urgent vascular surgery evaluation.

Aortic dissection extending into iliac/femoral vessels; popliteal artery entrapment syndrome (younger, athletic patients); hypercoagulable state (APS, HIT, malignancy); vasospasm (vasopressor-induced ischemia of toes/fingers in prolonged vasopressor infusions); trauma or iatrogenic injury.

Aortoiliac occlusion at aortic bifurcation: bilateral thigh/buttock claudication + absent femoral pulses + erectile dysfunction (classic triad). Often chronic but can present acutely. Requires aortoiliac reconstruction.

Prolonged vasopressor infusion (especially norepinephrine, vasopressin) causes vasospasm of distal arterioles → ischemia and necrosis of toes, fingers. Diagnosis of exclusion — ensure no proximal occlusion.

Deep vein thrombosis with phlegmasia (venous — limb is swollen/cyanotic, venous > arterial compromise); acute peripheral nerve injury; compartment syndrome (pain with passive stretch, tense compartment); severe Raynaud's; aortic dissection.

sections.title: Management
items: **Call vascular surgery immediately** — time to revascularization determines outcome. Do not delay the call waiting for imaging unless limb is clearly Class I.

**Anticoagulate immediately:** Heparin 80 units/kg IV bolus → drip at 18 units/kg/hr, titrate to PTT 60–80 (or per institutional protocol). Prevents propagation of thrombus; does not lyse the clot. Do NOT wait for imaging or surgery consult before starting heparin.
**Classify the limb** using Rutherford criteria (see above) — determines imaging strategy and urgency of OR.

**CTA angiography with runoff** (femoral → pedal): defines anatomy, level of occlusion, collateral flow, and inflow/outflow vessels for revascularization planning. Perform for Class I and IIa limbs. For IIb — go to OR; imaging in the OR if needed.
**Echo** if cardiac embolism is suspected (AFib, irregular rhythm, known LV dysfunction, valvular disease) — rule out LV thrombus, endocarditis. TEE > TTE for LA appendage thrombus.

**Revascularization decision (vascular surgery):** Catheter-directed thrombolysis (CDT) preferred for symptom onset <14 days, Class IIa; surgical embolectomy for IIb or failed CDT. Bypass grafting if native vessel disease. Primary amputation for Class III.

**Reperfusion injury monitoring** — after revascularization: metabolic acidosis (↑ lactate), hyperkalemia, myoglobinuria/ATN, compartment syndrome. Serial BMP, CK, urinalysis, compartment pressure checks.
**Fasciotomy** if compartment syndrome develops (compartment pressure >30 mmHg or within 30 mmHg of diastolic BP). Four-compartment lower leg fasciotomy is most common.

sections.title: Workup
items: **Labs:** CBC, BMP (Cr, K+), coagulation panel (PT/INR, PTT), T+S, lactate, CK, urinalysis (myoglobinuria), LFTs, hypercoagulable panel if no obvious cause (APS, protein C/S, antithrombin, Factor V Leiden — draw before anticoagulation if feasible)
**ECG:** Check for AFib, recent MI, arrhythmia
**CTA with runoff** (aorta to foot): level and extent of occlusion, collateral flow, disease in contralateral limb, and inflow/outflow for surgical planning. Gold standard for mapping.
**Duplex ultrasound / hand-held Doppler:** Bedside — documents arterial and venous signals, assesses for DVT. Serial exams track progression.
**Echo (TTE/TEE):** If cardiac embolism suspected — LV thrombus, LAA thrombus, wall motion abnormality, vegetation, PFO
**ABI (ankle-brachial index):** Abnormal <0.9; >1.3 implies calcified, non-compressible vessels (diabetics). For chronic PAD work-up, not acute diagnosis.

pairs.value: Preferred for Class IIa and select IIb with symptom duration <14 days. Catheter placed directly into thrombus; rtPA or urokinase infused. Takes hours to days — not for immediately threatened limbs needing salvage in minutes. Risk: bleeding, including intracranial hemorrhage (~1–2%).

Preferred for Class IIb, embolic ALI, or failed CDT. Balloon catheter thrombectomy under local or general anesthesia. On-table angiography after extraction ensures complete clot removal and identifies residual disease needing additional intervention.
For thrombotic ALI with underlying PAD and inadequate inflow/outflow after embolectomy. Femoropopliteal, femorotibial, or aortobifemoral bypass depending on anatomy.
Pharmacomechanical: aspiration + CDT for hybrid approach. Increasingly used in experienced centers. Reduces CDT time and drug dose.

For Class III (non-viable) limbs — revascularization in this setting risks fatal systemic reperfusion syndrome from release of massive metabolic load. Also for patients with prohibitive surgical risk.
Restoration of flow to ischemic muscle releases K+, lactic acid, myoglobin, and oxygen free radicals systemically. Severity proportional to duration and extent of ischemia.

Hyperkalemia (arrhythmia risk), metabolic acidosis, myoglobinuria → ATN and renal failure. Monitor BMP, ABG, CK, UA q4–6h post-revascularization. Aggressive IV hydration (1–1.5 mL/kg/hr), sodium bicarbonate in urine to alkalinize and prevent myoglobin precipitation.

Revascularized muscle swells → elevated compartment pressure → secondary ischemia. Presentation: pain disproportionate to exam, pain with passive stretch, tensely swollen extremity, paresthesias. Check compartment pressures (>30 mmHg or within 30 mmHg of diastolic BP). Fasciotomy is definitive treatment — do not delay.
Consider when: ischemia time >6 hours, large muscle mass involved, or intraoperative concern for ischemic swelling. Common after lower leg revascularization.

sections.title: Pearls & Pitfalls
items: **Emboli lodge at bifurcations** — most common sites: femoral bifurcation (most common), popliteal trifurcation, aortic bifurcation (Leriche), and brachial bifurcation in upper extremity.
**Lower limbs account for >80% of ALI.** Upper extremity ALI is much rarer and usually embolic from cardiac or subclavian/axillary aneurysm.

**Thrombotic ALI is typically less severe** — underlying PAD has allowed collateral vessels to form over time, providing partial perfusion. These patients often have a history of claudication and diminished contralateral pulses.

**Heparin does not lyse clot** — it prevents propagation and extension. Definitive treatment is always mechanical or thrombolytic removal. Do not delay calling vascular surgery while waiting for heparin to 'work.'
**'Better pain' can mean worse ischemia** — dense sensory nerve loss in non-viable limb can blunt pain. A patient who was in severe pain now reporting improvement may have progressed to Class III.
**Fixed mottling that does not blanch** = non-viable. Blanching mottling = still viable. Assess this with firm fingertip pressure at the bedside.

**On-table angiography** after surgical embolectomy is standard of care — confirms complete clot removal and identifies underlying disease. Residual defect = incomplete embolectomy or underlying stenosis requiring additional work.

**Vasopressor ischemia** — prolonged vasopressors (especially norepinephrine, vasopressin) can cause digital/toe ischemia in ICU patients. Check for proximal occlusion before attributing to vasospasm. Consider transition to alternate vasopressors and consultation.

**Screen chronic PAD with ABIs** — abnormal <0.9; >1.3 (non-compressible, calcified, common in DM) → segmental ABI with PVRs → CTA for revascularization planning. Classic claudication (exertional pain relieved by rest) is present in only 10–35% of PAD; atypical pain 40–50%; asymptomatic 20–50%.
**HIT** — if ALI occurs in a heparinized patient with thrombocytopenia, suspect HIT. Stop heparin immediately and switch to argatroban or bivalirudin.
**Compartment syndrome can occur even after successful revascularization** — monitor post-procedure for pain with passive stretch, tenseness, paresthesias.

drugs.name: Heparin (unfractionated)
drugs.dose: 80 units/kg IV bolus → 18 units/kg/hr infusion; titrate PTT 60–80 sec (q6–8h)
drugs.contraindications: Active major bleeding, HIT (switch to argatroban/bivalirudin)
drugs.notes: Start immediately on diagnosis — prevents propagation but does not lyse existing clot. Do not delay for imaging.

drugs.name: Alteplase (rtPA) — CDT
drugs.dose: 0.5–1 mg/hr intra-arterial via catheter (institutional protocol varies); max 24–48h
drugs.contraindications: Recent surgery (<10d), active bleeding, stroke within 3m, intracranial pathology
drugs.notes: Catheter-directed thrombolysis for Class IIa and select IIb ALI with <14 days symptoms. Check fibrinogen q4h; hold if <100 mg/dL.

drugs.name: Bivalirudin / Argatroban
drugs.dose: Bivalirudin: 0.15–0.2 mg/kg/hr; Argatroban: 2 mcg/kg/min; adjust to aPTT 1.5–3× normal
drugs.notes: For HIT-associated ALI or contraindication to heparin. Argatroban preferred in renal failure; bivalirudin preferred in hepatic failure.

drugs.name: Sodium bicarbonate (urine alkalinization)
drugs.dose: 150 mEq in 1L D5W at 100–200 mL/hr; target urine pH >6.5
drugs.notes: For myoglobinuria post-revascularization — alkaline urine reduces myoglobin precipitation in tubules and ATN risk.
